notes.b: Lifesaving (rescuing a person in difficulty in water) starts with decisions made before anyone enters the water. These four priorities shape every rescue.
points: The rescuer's own safety comes first, because a hurt rescuer cannot help the casualty (the person being rescued) and becomes a second person needing rescue.
Shout for help and alert the emergency services, so that trained help is on its way while you act.
Keep the casualty in sight at all times, because a casualty you lose sight of cannot be reached or guided.
Choose the safest method that will work, using the order of rescue methods, so you take on no more risk than the situation needs.
notes.tip: Rescuer safety comes first, and you should never recommend a contact rescue (physically touching the casualty) as the first option. Lifesaving appears in written answers on safe practice, roles, communication and first aid, so state the priorities in this order.

notes.h: Order of rescue methods, safest first
notes.b: Rescue methods run from the least risky for the rescuer to the most risky. Work down the list and stop at the first method that will work.
points: 1. Talk: shout instructions to the casualty. The rescuer stays on dry land and takes no risk.
2. Reach: extend an arm, a pole or a towel from the bank, so the casualty can grab it and be pulled in.
3. Throw: throw a buoyant aid (one that floats) or a rope for the casualty to hold.
4. Wade: enter the water on foot, only if it is safe to do so.
5. Row: use a boat to reach the casualty.
6. Swim: swim out and reach the casualty with an aid, which is riskier because the rescuer is now in the water.
7. Tow: a contact tow (the rescuer physically holds the casualty and swims them in), used only if the rescuer is trained and the tow is necessary, because it is the most dangerous method.
notes.tip: Learn the order talk, reach, throw, wade, row, swim, tow. Never recommend a contact rescue as the first option.

notes.b: Casualties differ in what they can do for themselves, and this decides how the rescuer approaches them. Four types are recognised.
points: Weak swimmer: a casualty who swims, but poorly, so may tire and get into difficulty.
Non-swimmer: a casualty who may panic and grab the rescuer, which puts the rescuer in danger.
Injured swimmer: a casualty who has been hurt in the water.
Unconscious casualty: a casualty who has lost consciousness and cannot help with the rescue, so the rescuer must do all the work.

notes.b: How a rescuer gets into the water depends on how much they know about its depth and clarity. A wrong entry can injure the rescuer, so the choice matters.
points: Slide-in entry: used for unknown depth or conditions, and the safest entry; the rescuer enters feet first and slowly.
Step-in entry: used in known depth and clear water, and keeps the rescuer's eyes on the casualty.
Straddle entry: used in known deep water, with the head kept above the water so the rescuer can watch the casualty.
Compact jump: a jump from a height into known deep water.
Unknown conditions: always enter feet first, slowly, while testing the depth, so the rescuer does not hit the bottom or hidden hazards.
notes.tip: Enter feet first into unknown water, and never dive.

notes.b: Once in the water, the rescuer must swim to the casualty without losing sight of them and without tiring.
points: Head-up front crawl (freestyle with the head kept out of the water) or head-up breaststroke keeps the casualty in sight during the approach.
Pace the approach to conserve energy for the return, because the swim back with the casualty is harder than the swim out.

notes.b: Towing a casualty means the rescuer's hands are busy, so the legs must do the work. Two techniques suit this.
points: The lifesaving kick is an inverted breaststroke kick (the usual breaststroke leg kick) performed on the back.
Sidestroke (swimming on one side) is also used for towing.
Both are used when towing, because the arms are occupied with the casualty or the aid.

notes.b: A frightened casualty can grab and drag a rescuer under. The final approach is therefore made carefully, from a distance.
points: Stop at a safe distance of about 2 to 3 metres from the casualty, so they cannot reach the rescuer.
Talk to reassure the casualty while stopped, which helps calm a panicking person.
Offer an aid, such as a rescue tube (a floating tube the casualty can hold) or towel.
If the casualty grabs the rescuer, submerge to break free.
notes.tip: Say "about" 2 to 3 metres when giving the safe stopping distance from a panicking casualty.

notes.b: A casualty facing the rescuer must be turned before towing, so that their breathing is protected.
points: From the front, turn the casualty onto their back.
Turn smoothly, keeping the casualty's face clear of the water.
The casualty's face is out of the water once they are on their back, so they can breathe during the tow.

notes.b: In a non-contact tow the rescuer never grips the casualty directly. Instead, an aid links the two of them.
points: The rescuer and the casualty both hold the aid, which keeps the rescuer out of reach of a panicking casualty.
Rigid aid (one that keeps its shape): a rescue tube or float.
Non-rigid aid (one that bends or folds): a towel or clothing.

notes.b: Where a casualty cannot hold an aid, the rescuer must hold the casualty directly. This carries more risk, so it is used only when needed.
points: Chin tow: the rescuer supports the casualty by the chin.
Cross-chest or arm tow: the rescuer holds the casualty across the chest or arm.
Keep the casualty's face clear of the water throughout the tow, so they can keep breathing.
Contact tows are used for tired or unconscious casualties, who cannot hold an aid themselves.
notes.tip: Never recommend a contact rescue as the first option. It comes last in the order of methods and is used only if the rescuer is trained and the tow is necessary.

notes.b: A rescue can be long, and the rescuer must still be able to reach safety. Four habits protect the rescuer's reserves.
points: Swim at a steady pace, so energy lasts the whole rescue.
Breathe regularly, so breath does not run out.
Rest on an aid when tired.
Minimise movement in cold water, because movement loses body heat.

notes.b: A rescue does not end when the casualty reaches the edge. Aftercare protects them once they are out.
points: Help the casualty out of the water with support.
Check the casualty's breathing.
Place the casualty in the recovery position, lying on their side to keep the airway clear.
Keep the casualty warm.
Seek medical help: a casualty rescued from water may still be at risk of secondary drowning (breathing problems that can develop after the rescue).
notes.tip: Written answers on lifesaving ask about first aid, so give breathing check, recovery position, warmth and medical help.

notes.b: A weak swimmer is in difficulty near the edge. This is the safest type of rescue, because the rescuer stays out of the water.
points: 1. Lie flat on the bank, so the rescuer is not pulled in.
2. Reach with a pole, or throw a buoyant aid.
3. Talk the casualty in towards the edge.

notes.h: Worked rescue: swimming rescue with an aid
notes.b: When the casualty is too far to reach or throw to, the rescuer swims out. This uses the entry, approach, tow and landing from the earlier blocks in order.
points: 1. Enter with a slide-in entry, feet first and slowly, testing the depth, because the conditions may be unknown.
2. Approach head-up, so the casualty stays in sight.
3. Stop about 2 to 3 metres from the casualty, talk to reassure them and offer the aid.
4. Tow the casualty with a non-contact tow, both holding the aid, using the lifesaving kick.
5. Land the casualty, helping them out with support.

keyTerms.definition: A slow, feet-first entry into water of unknown depth or conditions, the safest type of entry.
An entry into known depth and clear water in which the rescuer steps in and keeps their eyes on the casualty.
An entry into known deep water in which the rescuer's head stays above the water.
A jump from a height into known deep water.
A tow in which the rescuer and casualty both hold a rigid or non-rigid aid, keeping the rescuer out of reach.
A tow in which the rescuer holds the casualty directly, by the chin or across the chest or arm.
An inverted breaststroke kick performed on the back, used when towing because the arms are occupied.
A position with the casualty lying on their side to keep the airway clear.
A casualty who cannot swim and may panic and grab the rescuer.

factCards.term: Order of rescue methods, safest first
factCards.definition: Talk, reach, throw, wade (only if safe), row, swim with an aid, then tow (contact tow, only if trained and necessary).

factCards.term: Which entry keeps the head above water in known deep water?
How far should a rescuer stop from a panicking casualty?
factCards.definition: About 2 to 3 metres, then talk to reassure the casualty and offer an aid.

factCards.term: What does a non-contact tow use as its aid?
factCards.definition: A rigid aid such as a rescue tube or float, or a non-rigid aid such as a towel or clothing.

factCards.term: Aftercare after landing a casualty, in order
factCards.definition: Help out with support, check breathing, recovery position, keep warm, seek medical help.

questions.prompt: Describe the order of rescue methods a lifesaver should consider, and explain why the order matters.
questions.model: The order, safest first, is talk, reach, throw, wade (only if safe), row, swim with an aid, and tow. Talk and reach keep the rescuer out of the water altogether. Throwing a buoyant aid also keeps the rescuer on land while giving the casualty support. Wading, rowing and swimming with an aid each add risk to the rescuer, so they are used only when the earlier methods will not work and it is safe. A contact tow comes last because the rescuer is then in the water with a casualty who may panic and grab them. The order matters because the rescuer always chooses the method that gives the casualty the most help for the least risk to themselves.

questions.prompt: Describe a suitable entry into water of unknown depth and explain why it is used.
questions.model: The slide-in entry. The rescuer enters feet first and slowly, sliding into the water while testing the depth with the feet, so that they do not dive into shallow water or unseen obstacles. It is the safest entry because the rescuer finds the depth and any hazard before the head goes under, which avoids a head or neck injury from diving or jumping into unknown water.
